mainEntity.name: Can denture stomatitis go away on its own?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some mild cases, improving your denture hygiene routine and removing dentures overnight may help the condition to resolve. However, if the redness, soreness, or irritation persists, it is advisable to seek a professional dental assessment. Your dentist may recommend antifungal treatment or other interventions depending on the severity of the condition. Without proper management, denture stomatitis can become a recurring issue that may worsen over time. A clinical examination is the most reliable way to determine the appropriate approach.

mainEntity.name: How often should I clean my dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally recommended to brush your dentures at least once a day using a soft-bristled brush and a non-abrasive denture cleanser. Many dental professionals also suggest soaking dentures overnight in a suitable cleaning solution to help reduce microbial build-up. After soaking, always rinse your dentures thoroughly before placing them back in your mouth. Cleaning your gums, palate, and tongue daily is also important, as this helps remove residual plaque and supports the health of your oral tissue.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to sleep with dentures in?

acceptedAnswer.text: While it is physically possible to sleep with dentures in, it is generally not recommended. Wearing dentures continuously, particularly overnight, creates a warm and moist environment that promotes the growth of Candida and other micro-organisms. This significantly increases the risk of denture stomatitis. Removing your dentures at night gives the oral tissue an opportunity to rest and benefit from the natural cleansing effect of saliva. Your dentist can provide personalised advice based on your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Can I use regular toothpaste to clean my dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally advisable to avoid regular toothpaste for denture cleaning. Many standard toothpastes contain abrasive ingredients that can create microscopic scratches on the denture surface. These scratches provide additional areas where bacteria and fungi can accumulate, making the dentures harder to keep clean. Instead, use a denture-specific cleanser or mild soap alongside a soft brush. If you are unsure which products are best suited to your dentures, your dental team can recommend appropriate options.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my dentures fit properly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Well-fitting dentures should feel comfortable and stable during normal activities such as eating and speaking. Signs that your dentures may no longer fit well include increased movement or looseness, sore spots, difficulty chewing, or a clicking sound when talking. Over time, changes in the shape of your jawbone and gums are natural and can affect denture fit. If you suspect your dentures are no longer fitting correctly, arranging a dental assessment is advisable, as poorly fitting dentures can contribute to tissue irritation and increase the risk of conditions such as denture stomatitis.

mainEntity.name: Does denture stomatitis only affect upper dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture stomatitis is most commonly associated with upper dentures because the fitting surface of an upper denture covers the palate, restricting saliva flow to the tissue beneath. This creates the enclosed, moist conditions that are particularly favourable for fungal growth. However, the condition can occasionally affect the tissue beneath lower dentures as well, particularly if hygiene routines are insufficient. Regardless of which denture you wear, maintaining a thorough cleaning and storage routine is important for reducing risk and supporting oral health.
